passages.text:
Peter said, “You are saying impossible things. For even while he was coming into being little by little, he could have chosen to destroy him as an enemy himself. And, knowing beforehand that he would become not good, he would not have allowed it unless he knew that his coming into being would serve his own use. Nor was he capable of suddenly coming into being fully developed by himself, for someone who did not yet exist could not fashion himself. Nor can anything that has substance come into being out of what does not exist. And one could not rightly say that something that has come into being is equal in power to what always exists.”

Simon said, “Is it perhaps, then, one of the things that are relative, and is it evil in this way? It is bad, for example, as water is to fire, but good for ground that is untimely thirsty. Iron likewise is good for farming but bad for murders; desire, too, is not bad for marriage but is harmful for adultery. So also killing is bad, but good for the killer in relation to what he has planned. And greed is bad, but pleasant for the greedy person. Everything of this sort follows this pattern. By this argument, neither is evil evil, nor is good good, for each produces the other. Is it really the case that what seems to be done evilly brings delight to the doer but punishment to the sufferer? And if it seems unjust for someone who has loved himself to enjoy himself as much as possible, and because of this to suffer grievously at the hands of a righteous judge for having loved himself, to whom does it not appear unjust?”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὡς ἐχθρὸν ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ προαιρέσει ἀνελεῖν ἠδύνατο
lexical_decisions.chosen: he could have chosen to destroy him as an enemy himself
lexical_decisions.rationale: God remains the understood subject of ἠδύνατο. προαιρέσει specifies choice, and ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ is represented reflexively as personal agency, “himself.” Another attachment is “as an enemy brought into being by him”; the Greek arrangement does not make the attachment entirely unambiguous.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὔτε ἐξ οὐκ ὄντων γενέσθαι τί οὐσίαν ἔχει δύναται
lexical_decisions.chosen: Nor can anything that has substance come into being out of what does not exist
lexical_decisions.rationale: The supplied Greek has finite ἔχει (“it has”) beside δύναται (“can”), not a participle meaning “having” and not an expressed relative pronoun. I understand οὐσίαν ἔχει as a loose or parenthetic predication about the indefinite τί, “anything”: “nor can anything—it has substance—come into being out of what does not exist.” The main text integrates that predication into readable attributive English, “anything that has substance,” because the argument is discussing whether an existing being could arise from nonexistence. This is an English syntactic unpacking, not a change of the Greek to ἔχον or the insertion of a relative pronoun. A material alternative is to retain the parenthetic linkage, “Nor can anything—it has substance—come into being out of what does not exist.” That reading can assert substance of the particular posited being rather than limit the denial to a class of things that have substance. The Greek does not uniquely settle this linkage or scope. The negation and the supplied finite ἔχει are retained; the sentence is not harmonized with earlier competing claims about creation from nonexistence.

lexical_decisions.chosen: one of the things that are relative
lexical_decisions.rationale: πρός τι is the category of what is relative to something else; the supplied punctuation does not require a separate English clause. The following examples explicitly compare different effects on different recipients.
ἀκαίρως marks untimeliness or being out of season. “Ground thirsty at the wrong time” is an alternative; the adverb is not dropped as though the text merely said dry ground.
χαλεπή characterizes desire as difficult, harsh, or harmful in its adulterous use. “Troublesome” is possible but could understate the evaluative contrast.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: μήτιγε τὸ δοκοῦν κακῶς γίνεσθαι εὐφραίνει μὲν τὸν ποιοῦντα, κολάζει δὲ τὸν πάσχοντα;
lexical_decisions.chosen: Is it really the case that what seems to be done evilly brings delight to the doer but punishment to the sufferer?
lexical_decisions.rationale: μήτιγε ordinarily introduces a doubtful question or one leaning toward a negative answer. “Is it really the case that” preserves that questioning or doubtful force without changing the surviving proposition or making a flat assertion. Simon’s immediately preceding examples of pleasure for a wrongdoer and harm to a recipient also make an affirmative-leaning rhetorical interpretation contextually possible: “Does not what seems to be done evilly bring delight to the doer but punishment to the sufferer?” That alternative would solicit agreement with the relative-effects argument. The main text prefers the less leading doubtful wording because the question’s particle does not uniquely support the affirmative expectation; it does not claim that Simon’s intended answer is uniquely determined.

source_issues.source_quote: καὶ εἰ ἄδικον δοκεῖ τὸ ἑαυτὸν ἀγαπήσαντα. εὐφραίνειν ὡς δυνατόν ἐστι· καὶ διὰ τοῦτο χαλεπὰ πείσεσθαι ὑπὸ δικαίου δικαστοῦ περὶ τοῦ ἑαυτὸν ἠγαπηκέναι, τίνι οὐκ ἄδικον φαίνεται;
source_issues.issue: The wording has a difficult scope for the first “unjust”: the articular infinitive and subsequent infinitive can gather the self-pleasuring and its punishment into a single stated situation. The main text retains both occurrences of “unjust” and the positive “loved himself” rather than supplying a missing negation or turning the opening adjective into “just.” Another reading would take the initial description of injustice as Simon’s concession before his challenge about punishment. The supplied punctuation after ἀγαπήσαντα is not treated as a completed sentence.

passages.text:
Peter said, “One must discipline oneself through self-control whenever desire wants to rush toward another person’s harm, knowing that the evil one can destroy evil people, having received authority against them from the beginning. And so this is evil for those who have done evil. But that their souls remain under punishment after their destruction—this is indeed grievous, with someone rightly saying that the previously wrongly defined [one] is correct. For this reason, as I said, one must refuse to wrong someone else for the sake of a brief pleasure, so as not to bring oneself into everlasting punishment for the sake of a little pleasure.”

Simon said, “Is it perhaps, then, that there is nothing evil or good by nature, but the difference is a matter of law and custom ..̓̀.? Among Persians, marrying mothers, sisters, and daughters is a distinctive practice, whereas among others it is forbidden as something most grievous. Thus, since evils have not been defined for everyone, one cannot expect judgment from God.”

Peter said, “You cannot establish this. For it is apparent to everyone that having intercourse with mothers is abhorrent, even if Persians, who are one part of the whole, do not recognize the lawlessness of their abhorrent practice because of bad custom. So too Britons openly share with one another in front of everyone and feel no shame. Others eat human flesh and do not feel disgust, and others eat dogs’ flesh; still others do things that cannot be spoken of. Thus one must not make judgments by a perception that custom has diverted from what is natural. For being murdered is evil, even if not everyone says that no one wants to experience it himself; and no one takes pleasure in theft when it means his own punishment. So even if in any one case it is acknowledged that there are sins, we must necessarily and rightly also expect a third judgment concerning those sins.”

After Peter said this, Simon replied, “Is this how matters concerning the evil one seem to you? Tell me.”

lexical_decisions.rationale: The dative specifies the means of disciplining oneself. “Restraint” is another direct rendering.
ἀΐδιος explicitly conveys everlasting or eternal duration; the wording does not substitute “age-long,” and κολάσει is rendered punishment without making an additional claim about its purpose.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἴδιον τὸ γαμεῖν μητέρας, ἀδελφάς, θυγατέρας
lexical_decisions.chosen: marrying mothers, sisters, and daughters is a distinctive practice
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἴδιον means peculiar or distinctive to the people named. The main text translates the ancient speaker’s assertion without independently endorsing the historical ethnographic claim or adding erotic description.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὡς καὶ Βρεττανοὶ ἐμφανῶς ἐπὶ πάντων κοινωνοῦσι
lexical_decisions.chosen: So too Britons openly share with one another in front of everyone
lexical_decisions.rationale: κοινωνοῦσι means participate or share; an object such as wives or sexual partners is not explicitly stated. The contextual implication is left to the reader rather than supplied as surviving source wording.
The preceding σάρκας…ἐσθίουσι supplies the ellipsis; κυνῶν is the genitive “of dogs.”
The selected source expressly has τρίτην, “third.” No change to “future judgment” or other conjectural reading is made, although the enumeration is not explained in this passage.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ γὰρ τὸ φονευθῆναι κακόν ἐστι, κἂν μὴ πάντες λέγωσιν ὅτι μηδεὶς αὐτοπαθεῖν θέλει
lexical_decisions.chosen: For being murdered is evil, even if not everyone says that no one wants to experience it himself
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main text takes ὅτι as a content-clause marker after λέγωσιν: “say that.” Its immediate position after the verb of saying supports this ordinary linkage. On that analysis, the claim that no one wants to suffer murder is the content of a statement that is not universally made; Peter’s assertion that being murdered is evil precedes the concession. A material alternative takes ὅτι causally and attaches it to the assertion about murder’s evil: “For being murdered is evil, even if not everyone says so, because no one wants to undergo it himself.” On the causal reading Peter himself expressly gives the unwillingness to suffer murder as the justification for calling murder evil, while the concession concerns whether everyone acknowledges that evil. The following appeal to aversion to theft’s personal consequences makes that causal reading contextually plausible. The main content-clause reading is not claimed as uniquely settled, and neither reading changes the surviving negations.

source_issues.source_quote: τοῦτο ὄντως εἶναι χαλεπὸν δικαίως τὸν κακῶς προδιωρισμένον ὀρθῶς ἔχειν εἰπόντος
source_issues.issue: The construction can be read as a genitive absolute, εἰπόντος, with its speaker unexpressed: “with someone rightly saying.” δικαίως qualifies the saying; the accusative masculine τὸν κακῶς προδιωρισμένον is then the subject of the reported infinitive ὀρθῶς ἔχειν, “is correct” or “is in a right condition.” This analysis accounts for the surviving forms without emending the Greek or identifying an unexpressed speaker. The main text retains the unspecified masculine referent as “[one].” It could denote a person or being previously wrongly characterized; alternatively, with λόγον understood, it could mean a previously badly defined argument or account that is said to hold good. The Greek here does not name that referent or establish the speaker’s identity. “Wrongly defined” preserves κακῶς with προδιωρισμένον rather than changing it to “defined as evil.” The earlier concern was whether an intelligible grammatical construction could be supported at all; the implied-subject genitive-absolute analysis supplies one. The remaining referent and attachment uncertainty is disclosed rather than resolved by invention, so it is not treated here as an unreadable-source or missing-clause block. This remains a candidate interpretation requiring independent review.

The selected edition has two dots, accent marks, and a third dot after “custom.” The three dots and intervening marks are retained exactly as a printed gap; no conjunction or missing argument is supplied.

The square brackets mark supplied letters within words, not a dot-count lacuna. The supplied Greek is translated as printed (“forbidden as something most grievous”), and no additional conjectural letters are supplied.

source_issues.source_quote: κἂν οὖν ἑνὸς οὐδήποτε ὁμολογουμένου εἶναι ἁμαρτήματα
source_issues.issue: The construction is compressed: ἑνός is singular, while ἁμαρτήματα is plural, and οὐδήποτε is unusual in this position. “In any one case it is acknowledged that there are sins” takes ἑνός as one acknowledged instance and retains the plural sins. An alternative is “even if a single person anywhere acknowledges that there are sins.” The conclusion does not require specifying which referent of ἑνός is intended.
